facts: The Moon's far side gets sunlight too; far side does not mean permanently dark.
The Moon spins once per orbit, which is why the same face stays pointed toward Earth.
Humans first saw photographs of the Moon's far side from a Soviet probe in 1959.
Apollo astronauts brought back about 382 kilograms of lunar rocks and soil.
The Moon's dark seas are ancient lava-filled basins, not bodies of water.
The Moon's crust is thicker on its far side than on its near side.
Water ice survives inside permanently shadowed craters near the Moon's poles.
Your weight on the Moon would be about one-sixth of your weight on Earth.
The Moon once had a global ocean of molten rock.
Tiny meteorite impacts can release water trapped in the Moon's surface material.
The Sun contains about 99.8% of all the mass in our solar system.
The Sun's outer atmosphere is far hotter than its visible surface.
The Sun spins faster at its equator than near its poles.
Our whole solar system travels around the Milky Way, taking about 230 million years per circuit.
The Sun shines by fusing hydrogen into helium, not by burning like a campfire.
About 1.3 million Earth-sized volumes would fit inside the Sun.
The Sun's core reaches roughly fifteen million degrees Celsius.
Energy takes many thousands of years to work its way outward through the Sun's interior.
The Sun formed from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust about 4.6 billion years ago.
The Sun will eventually swell into a red giant, then leave behind a white dwarf.
Pluto has mountains built from water ice rather than ordinary rock.
Pluto's smooth plains include frozen nitrogen slowly churning like a very sluggish pot.
Seen from one side of Pluto, its moon Charon would stay in the same place in the sky.
Charon is about half Pluto's width, unusually large for a moon relative to its parent.
New Horizons gave us our first close-up look at Pluto in 2015.
Pluto was closer to the Sun than Neptune between 1979 and 1999.
Pluto's orbit takes about 248 Earth years to complete.
Pluto is smaller in diameter than Earth's Moon.
Pluto's four small outer moons tumble instead of always showing it the same face.
The moon Kerberos takes its name from the three-headed underworld dog of Greek mythology.
A comet can grow two different tails: one of dust and one of electrically charged gas.
A comet's tail is pushed away from the Sun rather than simply trailing behind its motion.
A comet's bright surrounding cloud can be vastly larger than its tiny frozen nucleus.
A warming comet's ice changes directly into gas, carrying dust with it.
Some sun-grazing comets break apart or evaporate during their close encounters.
Ancient Chinese records of comets still help astronomers study their appearances.
Comets preserve material left over from the formation of the solar system.
NASA's Stardust mission brought comet particles back to Earth in 2006.
NASA deliberately crashed an impactor into comet Tempel 1 to study material beneath its surface.
Some long-period comets take millions of years to complete a single orbit.
All the asteroids together have less mass than Earth's Moon.
Some asteroids have moons of their own.
Double asteroids can consist of two similarly sized rocks orbiting each other.
Some asteroids tumble through space instead of spinning neatly around one axis.
Being labelled a potentially hazardous asteroid does not mean a collision is predicted.
In 2022, NASA's DART impact changed the orbit of the asteroid moon Dimorphos.
The Chicxulub impact crater lies partly beneath the Yucatán region and nearby sea.
The 1908 Tunguska airburst flattened a vast area of Siberian forest.
A planet's gravity can nudge an asteroid into a very different orbit.
Infrared telescopes help astronomers find dark asteroids that reflect little visible sunlight.
A shooting star is a piece of space debris lighting up the atmosphere, not a falling star.
Some rocks found on Earth were blasted off the Moon or Mars by impacts.
Meteor showers recur when Earth crosses trails of debris left in space.
The Perseid meteors come from debris shed by comet Swift-Tuttle.
Most meteor-shower particles are only sand-grain to pea-sized.
Dark meteorites are easier to spot against Antarctica's ice than against ordinary rocky ground.
A meteorite's melted outer coating can form a thin, dark fusion crust.
Trapped gases can help identify a meteorite as a piece of Mars.
Most meteorites come from asteroids, not comets.
Iron meteorites are easier to recognise than stony ones, even though stony meteorites fall more often.
A black hole's event horizon is a boundary of no return, not a solid surface.
Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners; at a distance, their gravity behaves normally.
A black hole replacing the Sun with the same mass would leave planetary orbits essentially unchanged.
Gas swirling around a black hole can shine brilliantly even though the hole itself does not.
A black hole can bend the light of a more distant star like a gravitational lens.
Astronomers traced stellar orbits to demonstrate a massive black hole at our galaxy's centre.
Spaghettification describes the stretching caused by strongly unequal gravity near a black hole.
Colliding black holes send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves.
Some black holes form when massive stars collapse at the end of their lives.
The Milky Way's central black hole has about four million times the Sun's mass.
More massive stars generally die younger because they use their fuel much faster.
Some small stars can keep shining for trillions of years.
Stars begin inside cold clouds of gas and dust that collapse under gravity.
Young stars often form in groups called stellar clusters.
A newborn star can glow from the heat of collapse before nuclear fusion begins.
A star stays stable when outward pressure balances gravity pulling inward.
A white dwarf is a stellar remnant roughly the size of Earth.
Planetary nebulae are shed stellar material, despite having planets in their name.
Massive stars manufacture progressively heavier elements inside themselves.
A giant star's outer layers can expand while its core contracts.
